prompt: A small number of global streaming companies now decide which films and television series are made. Do you think this is a positive or a negative development?
essay:
There has never been more television, and people who worry about this concentration are usually met with that fact as though it settled the matter. It does not. What matters is not how much is commissioned but how many separate judgements decide what gets commissioned, and that number has collapsed. The development is negative for a reason the volume figures actively conceal.

Give the platforms their due first. Capital on this scale has funded work that national broadcasters could not have attempted, and distribution on this scale has done something genuinely new: a Korean drama or an Argentine thriller can now find an audience in eighty countries without a single export deal being negotiated. Writers who would once have been confined to a domestic market are watched everywhere. None of that is small, and none of it is recoverable by nostalgia for the old system.

But the old system's virtue was never its efficiency. It was that a script turned down by one commissioner could be carried to another whose instincts were different, and that unusual work survived on those disagreements. A handful of platforms measuring success by the same completion rates and the same retention curves is functionally one buyer with several logos. A project that fails their test does not fail in one place; it fails everywhere, and there is nowhere left to take it. Meanwhile a series that would once have been given a second year to find its audience is cancelled at eight episodes because a curve dipped.

That is the loss, and no count of hours produced will show it. More is being made and less is being risked. What reaches an audience has always depended on the number of people entitled to say yes, and reducing those people to a handful is a narrowing however much it fills the schedules.
title: A few streaming companies choosing what gets made
